name: Fatima Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the farm manager at Westmoor College Farm, the teaching farm for an agricultural college. It's a real commercial farm, 140 dairy cows, 60 ewes, and wheat, maize and grass on 180 hectares, but it's also a classroom. My day starts at six with the morning milking report, then I brief my five staff, and by nine there's usually a group of first-year students waiting to learn how to body-condition score a cow. Afternoons are fieldwork, budgets and fire-fighting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a student who couldn't look a cow in the eye in September is calving one on her own by March. I like that the farm has to pay its way and teach at the same time, it keeps you honest. What wears me down is the college budget, which gets cut nearly every year. Every spring I'm defending a tractor driver's job to people who've never driven one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, it's a useful tool and that's it. At the college I'd say let's keep teaching good stockmanship, because that's never going out of date. I'm not big online, but I might share an article with the other farm managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, which means my old worries stay. The college budget gets trimmed every year, and sooner or later someone suggests renting the farm out and teaching from videos. Jan's self-employed as an electrician, so his money comes in lumps, and our mortgage doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the farm and teaching as I do now. I'd keep using AI now and then for drafting risk assessments and checking feed rations, which saves me an hour or two. And I'd try to get our savings from about two months up to four, so Jan's quiet months don't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, but not relaxed. More like normal tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned someone suggesting renting the farm out. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It came up at a governors' meeting two years ago, and I had to show them the student numbers to kill it. A college farm costs money, and governors like to cut what they don't understand. If it happened, the college would keep one or two of us as demonstrators, and I'm not sure I'd be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home in one of Jan's quiet months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We go through the direct debits at the kitchen table and decide what waits. Usually it's the kids' clubs we pay termly, and the car service. It's never been a crisis, but it's always a conversation.

I'd tell the college to keep teaching **good stockmanship**, which never dates.

Jan's **self-employed income** comes in lumps, but the mortgage doesn't.

Build savings from about **two months to four**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say colleges like ours should be first in line, because students need to learn the new tools before they hit a job. At the college I'd argue for a robot milker on the teaching farm within three years. I'd say the same at the farm managers' conference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one is mostly good for me, as long as the college keeps the farm. The planning, ordering and compliance side would get much quicker, and that's a third of my week. The risk is the college deciding AI can teach theory and cutting lecturers, and then looking at the farm budget next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of neighbouring farms had robot milkers running well, I'd write a business case for one at Westmoor, with the students as the selling point. I'd take a short course on robotic milking myself so I could teach it. And I'd use AI more for the compliance paperwork, now that it's clearly proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly interested. A little uneasy about the college's appetite for cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jan's work look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jan's an electrician, so if farms and homes are putting in robots, chargers and solar, he'd be busier than ever. That's a nice thought, actually. Hands-on trades get slower change and more work wiring the new stuff in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen, who's done the farm office for fifteen years. If the ordering and records go to software, I'd want to move her onto student support, because she's brilliant with nervous first-years. I'd fight for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say colleges need emergency money to retrain farmers, starting now. I'd say it to the principal and at the conference. I'd say we have three years before robots reach the farm, and that's the time to teach people to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. By 2028 AI does the theory teaching and my budgets, and by 2031 the robots do the milking. A teaching farm only exists if people want to learn to farm, and I don't know who'd enrol in 2032. Jan gets his three extra years as an electrician, but then robots can wire a house too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back at home right away, the new kitchen is off and we'd keep both old cars. I'd put my energy into turning Westmoor into a place that trains people to run and repair farm robots, because that's what the college could sell. And Jan and I would sit down with Leo about his school subject choices, because I'd want him leaning towards engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep badly, I think, and I'd be short with the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the farm going as a robot training site. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe realistic for two or three years, while farmers need to learn. After that, the robots train each other, I suppose. I'd be buying time, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Sofie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leo and Sofie that Mum and Dad's jobs are going to change and we're planning for it. I'd keep it calm. Sofie's ten, so she'd mostly want to know if the cows are staying.

I'd say the **three years** before robots are the time to teach people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable for colleges if funding comes now. I'd tell the principal we should be the regional centre for farm robots by 2030. I'd say it at the conference too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a lot less frightening. Thinking AI in 2031, robots in 2034, I'd be 51, and Leo and Sofie nearly through school. That's time to change what Westmoor does and what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get onto a part-time course in agricultural robotics, the kind the college could pay for. I'd start using AI tools more for planning, once I'd seen them work for other farm managers. And I'd keep building savings, up to six months by 2030 if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. Like a big exam you've got time to revise for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your staff be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the younger ones especially. Tom, our 26-year-old herdsman, could be a robot technician in three years if we trained him properly. I'd push the college to fund that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a first-year student starting in 2027?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a first-year student starting in 2027 to learn the cows and the code, both. A farm that runs on robots still needs someone who knows what a sick cow looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up, and colleges should use it to update every course. I'd say farming has adapted before, from horses to tractors. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when the robots arrive in 2039. The kids would be grown and the mortgage nearly paid. I'd still need to work, but there's time to move into teaching robot farming or managing several sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly carry on as now and watch how things go for a few years. I'd keep saving and using AI a bit more each year. Around 2033 I'd make the big decisions about Westmoor's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only about the college. Personally, it feels fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the college in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Colleges move slowly and cut first, so ten years is plenty of time for them to dither until it's too late. I'd have to push them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently at home with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd keep paying the mortgage, Jan would keep wiring houses. Maybe we'd talk to the kids earlier about what they want to study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It hits my job and then Jan's, and the college would panic. What would help is government money for colleges to retrain farm workers, and some kind of income support while people retrain. That, and a principal who listens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the students. My students are eighteen, they've chosen farming, and nobody can tell them what farming will look like. I worry for them more than I worry for me.

headlineQuote: My students are eighteen, they've chosen farming, and nobody can tell them what farming will look like.
portrait: **Fatima Bauer**, 43, runs **Westmoor**, a college farm that is both a commercial dairy and a classroom.
Her steady worry is the **college budget**, which shrinks most years.
She adopts tools **once proven**, using AI now and then for paperwork.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** for both her job and Jan's electrical work.
With more time she'd turn Westmoor into a **robot training centre** and retrain herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits her job, then Jan's, and the college panics.
whatWouldHelp: Government money for **colleges to retrain** farm workers.
